title: A finitely generated unit quotient controls intersections of subfields
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with $0\ne1$, and let $K,L\subseteq A$ be subrings which are fields [def-weil-field], with the same identity as $A$. Write $A^\times$ for the group of units and identify $K^\times$ with its subgroup of nonzero elements of $K$. Suppose that the abelian quotient group $A^\times/K^\times$ is finitely generated, meaning generated by finitely many classes. Then the inclusion $K\cap L\subseteq L$ is a finite field extension: $L$ is finite-dimensional as a vector space over the field $K\cap L$. No assumption that $A$ is a domain, reduced, or finite type is imposed.

source.place: Tag 04MK (proposition-unique-base-field), quasi-compact case: inject the unit quotient of one subfield into the ambient quotient by the other, choose Laurent generators, and apply Zariski's lemma. This is only the ring-theoretic unit-quotient input, not scalar-field uniqueness.

proof.text: Put $F=K\cap L$. It contains $0,1$ and is closed under addition, negation and multiplication. If $0\ne x\in F$, its inverses in $K$ and $L$ agree in $A$, since an inverse is unique; hence $x^{-1}\in F$. Thus $F$ is a field [def-weil-field]. Every nonzero element of each of these fields is a unit of $A$, with the same inverse as in its field.

source.place: Tag 04MK, proposition-unique-base-field, quasi-compact case, paragraph beginning "Let $k_{12} = k_1 \cap k_2$" through the application of Algebra, theorem-nullstellensatz (00FV).

proof.text: Let $B=L^\times/F^\times$ and $Q=A^\times/K^\times$. These are abelian groups because $A$ is commutative. Define $j:B\to Q$ by $[\lambda]\mapsto[\lambda]$. Replacing $\lambda$ by $\lambda c$, $c\in F^\times$, does not change its class in $Q$, so this is a homomorphism. If $j([\lambda])=1$, then $\lambda\in K^\times\cap L^\times=F^\times$, so $[\lambda]=1$. Therefore $j$ is injective. Write $P=j(B)\subseteq Q$.

source.place: Tag 04MK, proposition-unique-base-field, quasi-compact case, paragraph beginning "Let $k_{12} = k_1 \cap k_2$" through the application of Algebra, theorem-nullstellensatz (00FV).

proof.text: Write $Q$ additively and choose finitely many generators $q_1,\ldots,q_r$ by the hypothesis. The homomorphism $\pi:\mathbf Z^r\to Q$, $(a_i)\mapsto\sum_i a_iq_i$, is surjective. Its inverse image $T=\pi^{-1}(P)$ is a subgroup of $\mathbf Z^r$. By [lem-weil-subgroup-finite-free-abelian-group-free], $T$ has a finite basis $t_1,\ldots,t_s$. For $p\in P$, surjectivity gives $t\in\mathbf Z^r$ with $\pi(t)=p$; then $t\in T$, so $p=\sum_j a_j\pi(t_j)$ for integers $a_j$. Thus the elements $\pi(t_j)$ generate $P$. Since $j:B\to P$ is bijective, their inverse images generate $B$.

source.place: Tag 04MK, proposition-unique-base-field, quasi-compact case, paragraph beginning "Let $k_{12} = k_1 \cap k_2$" through the application of Algebra, theorem-nullstellensatz (00FV).

proof.text: Choose representatives $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_s\in L^\times$ of these generators of $B$. For $\lambda\in L^\times$, there are integers $e_i$ with $[\lambda]=\prod_i[\alpha_i]^{e_i}$, so $\lambda=c\prod_i\alpha_i^{e_i}$ for some $c\in F^\times$. Each factor is a power of either $\alpha_i$ or $\alpha_i^{-1}$. Hence evaluation $F[X_1,\ldots,X_s,Y_1,\ldots,Y_s]\to L$, $X_i\mapsto\alpha_i$, $Y_i\mapsto\alpha_i^{-1}$, is surjective: this monomial gives every nonzero $\lambda$, and the zero polynomial gives zero. Consequently $L$ is a finite type $F$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra].

source.place: Tag 04MK, proposition-unique-base-field, quasi-compact case, paragraph beginning "Let $k_{12} = k_1 \cap k_2$" through the application of Algebra, theorem-nullstellensatz (00FV).

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-zariski-lemma] to the inclusion $F\hookrightarrow L$. Both rings are fields by the hypotheses and step 1, and step 4 supplies precisely finite generation as an algebra, rather than merely as a field. The conclusion is that $L$ is finite-dimensional over $F=K\cap L$, as required.
